Failure to Launch
FAYL-yer too LAWNCH
noun (Millennial slang)
Borrowed from rocketry (a launch that never leaves the pad), the phrase was popularized by the 2006 romantic comedy Failure to Launch, about a thirty-five-year-old man still living with his parents. It became shorthand, used by journalists and family therapists alike, for young adults who struggle to make the transition to independence: work, self-support, marriage, and a household of their own. It attached especially to Millennial men in the 2010s, as statistics on delayed marriage and living at home made headlines.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A failure to launch describes a young adult, often a young man, who never quite leaves the pad: still at home, underemployed or unemployed, without direction, marriage, or a household of his own, sometimes into his thirties. The phrase is half joke and half diagnosis. The Christian observation: Scripture has a clear picture of launching, and it is worth putting it beside the phrase. A man is meant to leave and establish: "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife" (Gen 2:24). He is meant to work: "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2Th 3:10). He is meant to grow up: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things" (1Co 13:11). Proverbs sends the stalled young man to the ant: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer" (Pro 6:6-8). Webster’s 1828 even uses the image: "to lanch into the wide world." At the same time, many young men who fail to launch are not simply lazy. Some are crushed by anxiety, some were never taught to work, and many were raised by screens and video games that offered achievement without risk. Fathers are part of the cure. "Train up a child in the way he should go" (Pro 22:6). A father who sees his son stalling does not merely scold; he gives him work, responsibility, a vision of manhood, and a push, and he prays that the Lord will make him a man who carries others.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial-era phrase (from rocketry; 2006 film) for young adults who do not transition to independence; Scripture’s pattern is leaving, working, and putting away childish things (Gen 2:24; 1Co 13:11), with fathers training sons to launch (Pro 22:6).

FAILURE TO LAUNCH, n. (Millennial-era phrase, 2006–present; from rocketry) The inability or failure of a young adult to achieve independence: steady work, self-support, and a household of his own.

Webster (1828), root lanch: LANCH, verb intransitive To dart or fly off; to push off; as, to lanch into the wide world; to lanch into a wide field of discussion.

Decode for parents: train for launch from childhood with real work and real responsibility; a stalled son needs a push and a vision, not just a scolding.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:24 — "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh."

2Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

1Co 13:11 — "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things."

Pro 6:6-8 — "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest."

Pro 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it."

Modern Corruption

Failure to launch names a real stall into adulthood, fed by sloth, fear, and a culture of risk-free distraction; Scripture calls men to leave, work, and put away childish things, and fathers to train them.

expand to see more

The corruption is prolonged adolescence. A culture that removes the expectations of adulthood, offers endless entertainment, and treats responsibility as optional produces men who drift. Video games provide the sensation of achievement without its demands; screens fill the hours that work would have filled. Some families make the stall comfortable. The result is not only economic but spiritual: men who never take up the burdens that would have made them strong.

The recovery is training and expectation. Boys should be given real work early, responsibility that matters, and a picture of manhood as service and sacrifice. Young men who have stalled need encouragement, structure, and sometimes a firm deadline. "It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth." Teach sons that the point of growing up is to carry others: a wife, children, a church, a community. That is a launch worth making.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French lancier (to throw a lance) → lanch / launch (to send forth; Webster 1828: "to lanch into the wide world") → rocketry → 2006 film → Millennial byword.

Late Latin lanceare → Old French lancier — to throw a lance

Webster 1828: lanch — to push off; "to lanch into the wide world"

20th c.: rocket launch; "failure to launch"

2006: the film Failure to Launch; 2010s: term for stalled young adults

Biblical anchor: when I became a man, I put away childish things (1Co 13:11); go to the ant, thou sluggard (Pro 6:6)

Usage
